reviews.text: TL;DR - Game just got released, buy it - ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ epic (Music, Gameplay, Items, SFX) - More Content coming soon - Dev is cool as ♥♥♥♥ - Totally not biased at all (not at all) [spoiler]I am a beta tester, got game for free, no other endorsement[/spoiler] [h1] General Overview [/h1] Against Great Darkness is a fun reimagining of the long forgotten brick-breaker genre. Made by a cool 40yr old with bad humor and a short attention span, this game allows you to play as a bunch of Pagan gods only Tumblr has heard of! Throw a frisbee at a cursed demon and watch it die, only to encounter a slot machine right after. Descend down (or rise out of?) Hell, through Dante's layers as Wu Kong, whilst utilizing the power of explosive disks, or maybe just a cheap knock off of Zeus, with a massive collection of Shiva memorabilia. Get screwed over by fun, and predictive bosses that make your male pattern baldness only grow with each playthrough [spoiler]nobody is safe from male pattern baldness... not even you.[/spoiler]. Risk your entire God run over a random chance "Event"? or just be a ♥♥♥♥♥ and heal yourself? The choice is obvious. Overall the game is very addictive, it's fun to just play more and more, to get juuuuusssst a few more motes for an upgrade, to beat one more another ascension, to finally unlock another pagan. Highly recommend for the price, with more updates and major features coming within [INSERT TIME THAT IS LESS THAN 3 YEARS], it's a pretty good investment. [h1] Content [/h1] Items? [i] ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. [/i] For a game of this size (relatively small), you have a BUNCH of items to choose from, resulting in some insane combos. Reminds me of Binding of Isaac in a way. Ascensions give you a linear difficulty increase while rewarding you with more shards to upgrade yourself [i](this is a roguelite afterall)[/i]. There is a slight lack of layers (only 3 as of writing), but more are in development, so I content is coming soon. [h1]Visuals / Sounds[/h1] I kid you not, this is game has some of the best soundtracks for a fresh indie game. Chai ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nailed the Music, and Duelysts along with Dirly made some incredible STX. Motivating, invigorating, hordes of enemies give you a slight sense of dread. Death music calms you down, bosses dying give you an auditory boner. Visually, Dirly knocked it out of the park (who knew that pixelart with a ♥♥♥♥ ton of post-processing looks good?) Not overwhelming, not agressive, just enough saturation to keep your eyes focused. very nice, i like. Each enemy looks distinct enough to recognize their threat at a glance, animations don't distract from gameplay. [spoiler]you also don't need a bitcoin mining setup to render this[/spoiler] [h1]Balancing[/h1] Over the months, the game has received multiple balance changes, a great majority being for the better, but some things just stay meta. As the game is right now, there are quite obvious meta's and "easy ways out", items that are just awful, but that is all up to the player's choosing. Some of the upgrades are also quite powerful, leading to an irreversible decrease in difficulty. Hopefully the future has something nicer in store. [h1]Mechanics[/h1] The game has very simple, but satisfying mechanics: movement is consistent and linear (unless you use controller), disk bouncing is somewhat predictable, cleanses are a simple spacebar tap. The tutorial does a great, [i]albeit very loud[/i] introduction to cleanses and fastballs. Less visible concepts like stats, juggles, item combinations are understood passively through gameplay. Anyone who has played a brickbreaker or space invaders will appreciate the identical mechanics. [h1]Meta[/h1] As mentioned previously, permanent upgrades and some meta Pagans/Items tend to steer gameplay towards a repetitive loop of: pick good pagan -> get good items -> win game -> upgrade to make loop easier -> repeat Again, this will be addressed in the future, but for now, just enjoy the stupid fun with items. This doesn't necessarily make the game bad, many games have metas, so maybe that's a good sign??? [h1]Conclusion[/h1] buy it.

Written on 4/17/2024, while the game is still in Early Access Against Great Darkness bills itself as a brickbreaker roguelike when it's really more of a juggling SHMUP roguelike. AGD is too chaotic to consistently hit enemies with balls (called "discs" in game), and so the player is forced to rely on weaker secondary weapons, and using special attacks and abilities that are triggered by juggling discs consecutively without dropping them. The challenge is supposed to lie in dodging enemy attacks to consistently juggle discs, and this is challenging, but the discs themselves can collide with each other, which fairly regularly results in my ship spawning a disc while I'm lined up to intercept another, sending both careering down. Furthermore, most of the upgrades available to the player enhance the secondary weapons, and not the discs themselves. In order to aid the player in juggling balls, the game offers the player a "cleanse" ability, which can remove enemy projectiles a limited number of times per level. However, the cleanse is almost entirely useless, as enemies themselves will often charge downscreen past the player, and cannot be cleansed. One can only attempt to clear the enemies before they are too close, which can also often result in the enemy being cleared after it has begun its charge, and spiking the ball straight down past the player, ruining the juggle streak. Unfortunately, even though the game teaches the player that the balls are less useful than weapon attacks rather quickly, it also forces the player to rely on the balls for at least one boss battle, and later introduces enemies with an invulnerability-to-weapon-damage aura. After clearing a level, the game offers the player a number of rewards, including the ability to take a random "event." It's made almost immediately clear to the player that the events are almost always less good than just stockpiling currency to go to the shop later. Furthermore, the very first "prestige" level the player unlocks introduces negative events, which just reinforces that the player should never ever take an event in the first place. The game uses a rather baffling combo of keyboard and mouse - the player'ss movement is strictly keyboard only, with either A/D or the left and right arrow keys, but cleanses can be triggered by either spacebar or LMB. Menus can be navigated with keyboard and spacebar, but this more clunky than just switching back to the mouse. The whole experience would be smoother if the player followed the mouse cursor and the whole game could be played with just the mouse. I assume this game was developed for controller, which is a sticking point for me - if you're going to release a game on a platform, you should support its default peripherals. The game is very pretty. Unfortunately, for at least one character, it means the player has to fight the aesthetic. There is one unlockable character who shoots a pale white laser beam straight up. Unfortunately, everything the player fires is plain white, including both the laser and the discs, meaning it's almost impossible to see the discs coming down in the laser beam. I can't help but compare the gameplay of this to another retro-roguelike called Peglin. Where Peglin embraces its peggle roots and takes the genre in new and interesting ways by introducing balls that act differently, AGD treats its brick-breaking heritage as a limitation that it isn't quite clear which direction to go with. It would be a better game if it dropped the ball-juggling gimmick and focused strictly on being an aesthetic SHMUP roguelike.

This feels like a full release. A small full release, but still a full release. But it is not, it is in early access and it offers great value for its money. I will say that you have to at least be somewhat comfortable with the concept of bullet hell and with not blinking for minutes on end. But otherwise I can highly recommend the game to everyone. Give the (prologue) demo a try, you will figure out quickly if you can get into it. I have played over 20 hours now, cleared all difficulty levels and finished 80% of its achievements and all I want is more game. There is still some balance needed, but that will come with time and feedback, there is no glaring balance issues.

February 6, 2025: I can't recommend this game anymore. A game in Early Access is meant to receive feedback, updates, etc. until it becomes fully released. However, there hasn't been any updates or notes from the developer in a long while. As a result, I have no choice but to label this as abandonware. Don't get me wrong: it's a fun game, but if this is meant to be the final version, I can't recommend buying it. April 21, 2024: So far, so good. Imagine Vampire Survivors meets Touhou. This game is, in my opinion, a raw gem that is slowly being polished. There are some things that I believe would make things better for QoL purposes (such as counting disks hitting each other as a juggle, or allowing a delay in cleanse so that you can "cleanse" a hit if you react fast enough), but this is a work in progress. For now, this is my go-to game when I have less than an hour to play something.

As an Early Access title this is honestly a wild amount of content and potential. The interactions of abilities and unique characters makes this a ton of fun. I can't wait to see how this evolves over time if this is the initial offering.

Surprisingly addicting. I dig it. Hoping for more levels/higher difficulty in the future, but even if not, this will be on my list of go-to daily games. I'm typically an Isaac kind of guy, and this tickles the same rogue-like aspect. Buy items wisely, aim for synergies, and have yourself a time. At 13 hours played, I've only really broken the game once (by this I mean doing so much damage that waves are instantly melting). I think i had 50+ discs on screen. Every other run has been fairly well-balanced. I beat 95% of the runs I play. I'd like this to be lower. Challenge me! Give me an insane difficulty where i only win 10-20% of the time. I might be in the bottom percentage of players with this mindset, and I am willing to accept that I probably won't get this. ...but I'll still play. It's fun as hell. 7

Against Great Darkness is a roguelite action game developed and published by Hitreg Studios that stands out through its willingness to experiment with genre conventions. While many roguelites borrow familiar ideas from twin-stick shooters, dungeon crawlers, or survival games, this title takes inspiration from an entirely different source by incorporating brick-breaker mechanics into a fast-paced battle against the forces of Hell. The result is a surprisingly creative blend of arcade action, strategic build crafting, and chaotic combat that feels fresh even within a genre filled with innovative concepts. The premise places players in the role of legendary pagan heroes and deities who find themselves trapped in the underworld. Their goal is straightforward: survive relentless demonic assaults and carve a path toward freedom. Although the narrative remains relatively simple, the setting provides an entertaining backdrop for the action. The game embraces themes drawn from mythology and religious imagery, creating an environment filled with monstrous enemies, dangerous bosses, and strange supernatural encounters. This combination gives the adventure a distinctive identity that separates it from more traditional fantasy roguelites. What truly defines the experience is its combat system. Instead of focusing exclusively on weapons and projectiles, players must manage magical disks that bounce around the battlefield and inflict damage on enemies. These disks function similarly to the ball in a classic brick-breaker game, but their integration into a roguelite shooter creates an entirely different dynamic. Success requires constant awareness of enemy positions, incoming attacks, and the movement of the disks themselves. The battlefield often becomes a whirlwind of projectiles, effects, and ricocheting attacks, creating a frantic but satisfying rhythm. As players progress through runs, they collect relics and upgrades that dramatically influence gameplay. These enhancements can alter the behavior of disks, strengthen attacks, increase survivability, or create powerful interactions between various abilities. Discovering effective combinations becomes one of the game's most rewarding features. Some builds focus on overwhelming offensive power, while others emphasize survival or utility. The constant search for stronger synergies encourages experimentation and ensures that no two runs feel exactly alike. The roster of playable characters further expands the game's replay value. Each hero possesses unique strengths, weapons, and attributes that significantly change how battles unfold. Some characters excel at aggressive combat, while others require a more calculated approach. Learning how each character interacts with different relics and upgrades adds another layer of depth to the progression system. This variety helps maintain player interest over the long term and provides compelling reasons to continue unlocking content. Enemy design contributes greatly to the challenge. Demonic creatures attack from multiple directions, often filling the screen with projectiles and hazards that demand precise movement. The game steadily increases the intensity of encounters as players advance deeper into Hell, ensuring that each new area introduces fresh threats and tactical considerations. Random events and unexpected encounters also add variety, preventing runs from becoming predictable and forcing players to adapt to changing circumstances. Boss encounters represent some of the most exciting moments in the game. These battles combine all of the mechanics introduced throughout a run and test the player's mastery of movement, positioning, and build optimization. Managing bouncing disks while avoiding deadly attack patterns creates encounters that feel both challenging and rewarding. Victories are earned through skillful play rather than simple numerical advantages, making successful boss defeats especially satisfying. Visually, Against Great Darkness adopts a retro-inspired style that prioritizes readability and gameplay clarity. The graphics may appear simple at first glance, but the clean presentation works well during the most intense battles. Enemy attacks remain easy to identify, environmental hazards are clearly visible, and the action never becomes overly cluttered despite the large number of effects on screen. This design philosophy allows players to focus on strategic decision-making without being distracted by unnecessary visual noise. The game's audio complements the action effectively. Energetic music accompanies the increasingly frantic combat, while impactful sound effects provide satisfying feedback during battles. Together, the audiovisual elements create an atmosphere that reinforces the feeling of fighting through a hostile and dangerous underworld. The fast pace of the soundtrack helps maintain excitement throughout extended play sessions. The game's largest obstacle is its complexity. New players may find themselves overwhelmed by the number of systems operating simultaneously. Managing disk trajectories, understanding relic interactions, avoiding enemy attacks, and building effective strategies can require a significant adjustment period. Those expecting a simpler arcade experience may initially struggle with the learning curve. However, players who invest the time to understand its mechanics will uncover a remarkably deep and rewarding roguelite. Against Great Darkness succeeds because it takes risks where many games choose familiarity. Its unusual fusion of brick-breaker mechanics, roguelite progression, mythological themes, and bullet-heavy combat creates an experience that feels genuinely original. While it may not appeal to every player due to its demanding systems, it offers a level of creativity and replayability that is increasingly rare. For fans of challenging roguelites who enjoy experimenting with builds and mastering unconventional mechanics, this journey through Hell delivers a memorable and highly engaging adventure. Rating: 7/10
